html:
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was the first inter-city railway in the world, opened on 15 September 1830 between the port of Liverpool and the cotton town of Manchester in north west England. It was the first line to run only on steam locomotives, to a timetable, carrying both passengers and goods. The railway age began with it.

Manchester's mills needed raw cotton from Liverpool's docks, and the canals that carried it charged high rates and were slow. Merchants backed a railway, against fierce opposition from canal owners and landlords. George Stephenson was the engineer. The line crossed a large peat bog, Chat Moss, on a floating bed of brushwood and earth, and ran through deep cuttings and a long tunnel into Liverpool.

Key moments:

  • The Rainhill Trials of 1829 picked the locomotive. Robert Stephenson's Rocket won, and its design, with many fire tubes in the boiler, set the pattern for later engines.
  • The opening day was marred when the politician William Huskisson was hit by Rocket and died, among the first widely reported railway deaths.
  • Passengers, not expected to matter much, soon made up much of the income.

It used the high pressure steam that James Watt had avoided in his steam engine, and it was a commercial success. Within twenty years Britain built thousands of miles of railway, and the model spread across Europe, the Americas and India. Railways made national markets, standard time and cheap travel, and fed the cotton economy and the wider Industrial Revolution.
